comparison: Both strongly support the development of the annotation workflow and database resource (C2, C3, C24, C121, C122). OpenEval focuses on technical methodology details, while peer reviewers emphasize the community value, calling it 'an unparalleled community resource' and 'a welcome addition.' Both also address the quantitative scope (C4, C36, C37 in OpenEval; C25, C26 in peer review).

OpenEval R2 evaluates quantitative prediction results (C4, C36, C37, C38, C40) as SUPPORTED with focus on technical details. Peer R1 includes some of these claims (C4, C36, C37) as part of broader affirmation of the pipeline and database, emphasizing community resource value rather than specific technical metrics.

Both support the shadow enhancer simulation findings (C5, C45-C49). OpenEval provides detailed statistical assessment (p<0.001, appropriate methodology), while peer reviewers accept these as part of 'independent comparisons' that 'creatively draw on existing resources' to validate predictions. Both find the evidence convincing.

Perfect claim overlap (C6, C50-C53). Both support the orthology analysis findings. OpenEval acknowledges limitations in ortholog calling while affirming statistical significance. Peer reviewers accept this as evidence for 'identifying functional enhancers across large phylogenetic distances,' implicitly endorsing the cross-species prediction capability.

Perfect claim overlap (C7, C54-C61). Both support the chromatin accessibility validation approach. OpenEval notes highly significant p-values and substantial fold enrichments while acknowledging tissue mismatches. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as 'independent comparisons...with chromatin accessibility data' that strengthen conclusions.

Both address in vivo validation (C8, C62-C65, C87-C88), but with different evaluation types. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with 77% validation rate. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting 'field-wide lack of independently validated set' and cautioning that 'output should be regarded as another prediction-generating tool,' expressing reservations about generalizability despite accepting the data.

Perfect claim overlap (C66-C71). Both rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes these are 'reasonable hypotheses' but 'untested in this study.' Peer reviewers implicitly acknowledge limitations through overall caution, with editor noting 'experimental validation is not yet available in the field' for such evolutionary distances, though they don't explicitly discuss these specific caveats.

Both support the ex locus validation results (C91-C95). OpenEval provides detailed species-specific analysis noting mixed results. Peer reviewers accept these as part of validation dataset, with editor noting 'functional validation through reporter gene analysis strengthen their conclusions,' accepting both positive and negative outcomes.

Both support klu locus validation (C97-C99). OpenEval documents clear D. melanogaster activity and weaker results in other species. Peer reviewers accept these experimental results as supporting evidence within the broader validation framework, acknowledging the mixed outcomes strengthen rather than weaken conclusions.

Both support ush locus validation (C101-C103). OpenEval notes mixed results across species with functional enhancers identified in two of three species. Peer reviewers accept these as part of validation dataset, implicitly endorsing the interpretation that mixed results are expected and informative.

Both support hth locus validation (C104-C107). OpenEval emphasizes strong T. castaneum correspondence with known expression patterns. Peer reviewers accept these experimental results as part of overall validation approach, including negative A. aegypti result as appropriately documented.

Both support Ubx validation results (C109-C113). OpenEval notes tissue-specific activity patterns consistent with known Ubx expression. Peer reviewers accept these experimental results, with overall acceptance of validation approach indicating endorsement of both positive findings and ectopic expression observations.

Both support psq locus validation (C116-C118). OpenEval notes lower success rate (one of three predictions active) but clear documentation. Peer reviewers accept these results as part of validation dataset, with acceptance of mixed outcomes across all tested loci indicating these results strengthen overall conclusions.

Both address overall prediction accuracy estimates (C87-C89). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with 50-85% range based on multiple validation approaches. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, accepting the data but expressing caution about generalizability, stating predictions 'should be combined with other sources of evidence to be practical.'

Both support SCRMshaw cross-species capability (C23, C27, C28 overlap; R16 includes broader methodology C21-C33). OpenEval emphasizes established prior validation. Peer reviewers find 'cross-species analysis...interesting' and affirm 'uses in identifying functional enhancers across large phylogenetic distances,' supporting the core methodological foundation.

High claim overlap (C39-C42). Both support the handling of prediction size artifacts. OpenEval emphasizes honest reporting and minimal impact of filtering outliers. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these technical details through overall acceptance of methodology and database resource.

Both support interpretation of negative results and adult_PNS training set performance (C74-C75). OpenEval documents poor performance across multiple metrics with appropriate caution. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through overall acceptance of simulation analyses, though they don't explicitly discuss this specific biological interpretation.

Partial overlap on shadow enhancer biology (C76-C78) and inference about regulatory mechanisms (C79-C81). OpenEval supports novel inference about similar regulatory mechanisms. Peer reviewers implicitly support through acceptance of shadow enhancer findings, though they don't explicitly discuss this specific biological interpretation.

Partial overlap on regulatory mechanism inference (C79-C81) and future research implications (C82). OpenEval supports these as logical inferences from SCRMshaw results. Peer reviewers accept cross-species prediction capability and note the approach's utility for future research, aligning with these interpretations.

Both support acknowledgment of limitations and resource utility (C83-C86, C89). OpenEval emphasizes honest assessment of orthology analysis limitations while demonstrating statistical significance. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge resource utility despite limitations, stating it 'will be a welcome community resource' and should be 'combined with other sources of evidence.'

Both support framing resource as preliminary (C86). OpenEval notes this is consistent with standard genome annotation practices. Peer reviewers affirm the database 'will be a welcome community resource in its current state, and even more so as the authors continue to expand their annotations,' accepting the ongoing improvement framework.

OpenEval evaluates technical observation about basal activity in control lines (C119-C120) as SUPPORTED, noting honest reporting of limitation affecting embryonic results interpretation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific technical detail.

OpenEval evaluates methodological parameters (C34-C35) as SUPPORTED, noting clear documentation for reproducibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific technical parameters.

OpenEval evaluates background context and motivation (C1, C9-C20) as SUPPORTED, noting effective context-setting though primarily established knowledge rather than novel findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this background material.

OpenEval evaluates phylogenetic and temporal scope descriptive statistics (C25-C26) as SUPPORTED. While peer R1 includes C25-C26, it focuses on broader pipeline affirmation rather than specifically evaluating these scope statistics.
